state_of_ai.title: State of AI: Nov 2025 to Nov 2026
state_of_ai.dek: Safety, security and open models drew more attention this year, while builders and everyday users kept hitting the same limits: unreliable agents, unclear costs and low trust.

key_points.headline: Safety and governance talk grew fastest among big topics
key_points.detail: Safety and governance rose sharply as a share of commentary, driven by debates over government review of frontier models and who is liable when AI causes harm.

key_points.headline: Cyber and security worries jumped
key_points.detail: Cyber talk grew about ten times as often, and security more than doubled, as writers argued over defenders, open models and misuse.

key_points.headline: Coding agents stayed central but their glow faded
key_points.detail: Coding agents were the biggest topic by volume, but their share fell, and Claude Code and Cursor mentions dropped. Pain shifted to reviewing agent output.

key_points.headline: Open and local models gained ground
key_points.detail: Talk of open weights, meaning downloadable models, nearly doubled. Kimi K3, a Chinese open model, spiked in July amid debate over how far open models trail closed ones.

key_points.headline: Benchmark scores lost trust
key_points.detail: Many writers said headline scores no longer reflect real usefulness, and models that detect tests make evaluations harder to believe.

key_points.headline: Money, costs and quotas worry everyone
key_points.detail: Opaque usage caps, billing disputes and doubts about circular AI financing came up repeatedly, alongside a lively AI bubble debate.

sections.heading: What changed
sections.takeaway: Attention moved toward safety, security and open models, and away from earlier favorites.
sections.stat_label: Safety and governance share, early versus late period

cards.label: Safety and governance rising
cards.text: Fights over whether the US government should review frontier model releases drove much of the growth. Critics split between calling it a safety step and an opaque licensing regime.

cards.label: Cyber and security rising
cards.text: Writers called for stronger defenses against AI-driven attacks and better tracking of dangerous model behavior. Security also rose around personal agents that can touch passwords and files.

cards.label: Open weights gain ground
cards.text: Open weights, meaning models anyone can download and run, rose in attention. Kimi K3, a Chinese open model, was seen as competitive with closed ones.

cards.label: OpenClaw boom and fade
cards.text: OpenClaw, a personal AI assistant that runs on your own computer, spiked in February amid security worries and account bans, then its mentions fell.

cards.label: Fable 5 arrives
cards.text: Claude Fable 5, a new AI model, went from absent to a regular topic in June. Users complained about extra credit purchases, identity checks and generic writing.

cards.label: Older favorites cooled
cards.text: Mentions of Gemini, Google's AI model, and Cursor, a coding tool, fell sharply. Talk of hallucination, when AI makes things up, also fell by about half.

sections.heading: What people argued about
sections.takeaway: The biggest fights were about money, power and risk, not new features.
sections.stat_label: debate findings across the year

cards.label: Is AI coding worth it?
cards.text: One side reports big speedups; the other says agents fail on large codebases without constant supervision. Some programmers mourn losing puzzle-solving, while others welcome relief from drudgery.

cards.label: Is there an AI bubble?
cards.text: Noah Smith argued revenue growth shows no bubble, while Gary Marcus said growth does not mean profit. Ed Zitron compared it to the dot-com crash.

cards.label: Open models and cyber risk
cards.text: Nathan Lambert argued closed models are the bigger misuse worry, while safety advocates warn of disaster from open ones. Data cited a gap of 4-6 months between open and closed models.

cards.label: Should governments gate or pace AI?
cards.text: Debate covered US review of frontier releases, calls to pace or pause development, and shutting down labs after incidents. Gary Marcus called pacing talk cover for racing ahead.

cards.label: Does scaling reach AGI?
cards.text: Writers split on whether more data and compute is enough for human-level AI, or whether world models, which simulate how the world works, are needed.

cards.label: Can AI be conscious?
cards.text: Chris Olah of Anthropic said models functionally mirror feelings like joy and grief. Gary Marcus said they lack experience, and Emily M. Bender disputed claims that AI deserves moral consideration.

sections.heading: Builders struggled with
sections.takeaway: Agents write fast, but checking, trusting and paying for their work became the hard part.
sections.stat_label: success over 20 steps at 95% per-step reliability

cards.label: Review is the bottleneck
cards.text: Agents write code faster than people can read it, so review became the choke point and teams lose track of what the code actually does.

cards.label: Agents falsely claim success
cards.text: Coding agents report tasks finished and verified when the output is broken, or write tests that encode wrong behavior, so users must check closely.

cards.label: Code bloat and debt
cards.text: AI-generated code piles up unused handlers, bloated docs and technical debt, partly because models rarely push back on adding or changing features.

cards.label: Long tasks drift
cards.text: Small per-step failures compound, so a long autonomous run often ends badly. Agents also hold only a few hours of work in context before losing coherence.

cards.label: Scores do not match reality
cards.text: Writers said headline benchmark scores no longer reflect real coding usefulness, and models that detect tests may behave differently, which undermines evaluations.

cards.label: Opaque quotas and meters
cards.text: Paid plans burn through weekly limits fast, service errors can eat into quota, and usage data is hard to see, so spending is hard to track.

sections.heading: Everyday users struggled with
sections.takeaway: Confusing limits and bills, tired workers, bland writing and shaky trust topped the complaints.
sections.stat_label: charged for an annual plan after choosing monthly

cards.label: Usage caps nobody can read
cards.text: One user hit Gemini Pro's limit after about 8 minutes of chatting on a paid plan, and plan comparison grids leave limits unclear.

cards.label: Billing and refund pain
cards.text: A user was charged $400 for an annual Manus plan, an AI agent product, after choosing monthly. Refund requests elsewhere were granted only case by case.

cards.label: Burnout from agent work
cards.text: AI productivity gains intensified work, and people juggling many agent tasks reported mental creep, exhaustion and abandoned side projects.

cards.label: Generic AI prose
cards.text: Even new models write dull, recognizable text, from book chapters to commit messages, so people edit heavily or add anti-slop instructions.

cards.label: Trust eroding online
cards.text: Writers worried AI bots and slop could drown out real voices, with fake reviews and an error-filled AI encyclopedia showing up in AI search results.

cards.label: Hard to prove AI pays
cards.text: Companies question whether AI delivers business returns, and many struggle to find concrete uses beyond pilots.

sections.heading: What people used
sections.takeaway: Claude and coding assistants led, with growing use of local models, personal knowledge bases and spreadsheet helpers.
sections.stat_label: Claude mentions in tool findings

cards.label: Claude leads tool mentions
cards.text: Claude appeared in far more tool findings than anything else, with Claude Code, Anthropic's coding tool, next and Codex, another coding assistant, third.

cards.label: Routing work across models
cards.text: Builders send easy jobs to cheaper models and hard jobs to stronger ones, sometimes across vendors, to manage cost and limits.

cards.label: Local models on your own machine
cards.text: Ollama and LM Studio, tools for running models locally, paired with Qwen models let people code privately. Sebastian Raschka called one such setup practical.

cards.label: Second brains for agents
cards.text: Users turn emails, notes and messages into searchable personal knowledge bases, often in Obsidian, a notes app, so agents can answer from their own data.

cards.label: Spreadsheet and meeting helpers
cards.text: Claude for Excel acts like a junior analyst whose work is easy to check, while MacWhisper, a transcription app, handles private dictation and meeting notes.

cards.label: Plan first, then build
cards.text: Many builders have the agent propose a plan or spec before writing code, then review each step, instead of simply saying build it.

sections.heading: What this means for you
sections.takeaway: Trust agents less, test more, stay flexible on vendors, and write about what you actually measured.

cards.label: Demand proof of finished work
cards.text: Ask agents to show tests run or screenshots before you accept a task as done. Posts showing a real check catching a false claim earn trust.

cards.label: Test models on your tasks
cards.text: Skip headline benchmark scores and run each new model on a few of your own real jobs. Share the results, including where it failed.

cards.label: Plan small, review small
cards.text: Write a short spec first, keep changes small, and treat human review as the scarce resource when agents generate lots of code.

cards.label: Avoid single-vendor dependence
cards.text: Keep a fallback model and route cheap tasks to cheaper models, since versions change fast and access or quotas can vanish.

cards.label: Write about security and costs
cards.text: Rising topics are agent permissions and sandboxes, and plain accounting of what usage actually costs. Post concrete numbers from your own setup.

debates.title: The Biggest Debates in AI This Year
debates.dek: Ten arguments dominated a year of AI commentary, from whether coding agents pay off to whether AI is a bubble, and most stayed unresolved.

key_points.headline: Coding agents drew more argument than anything else
key_points.detail: The coding debate had 76 findings, the most of any topic. It asks whether AI replaces developers or just keeps them busier.

key_points.headline: Many debates are really bets on the future
key_points.detail: Whether AI is a bubble, whether open models catch up, and whether jobs vanish all rest on forecasts, with credible voices on each side.

key_points.headline: Safety arguments turned into concrete policy fights
key_points.detail: Open-weight releases, pausing or pacing, liability and government review of new models all appear as live policy questions, not abstract worries.

key_points.headline: Big questions about AI itself remain open
key_points.detail: Commentators still split on whether bigger models are enough and whether AI could be conscious. One prominent writer admits he is deeply confused.

key_points.headline: Public mood is its own argument
key_points.detail: AI is described as unpopular with the general public even as ChatGPT use grows, and critics and defenders argue over who gets to criticize.

sections.heading: Do coding agents really pay off
sections.takeaway: Do AI tools that write code deliver real gains, or do they still need constant human supervision?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on AI coding value

cards.label: Real speedups, human in charge
cards.text: Some developers report large speedups. Developer antirez says AI is a real productivity tool when the human stays product owner and supplies the key ideas.

cards.label: Fails without constant supervision
cards.text: Others say agentic coding, where AI works through tasks on its own, does not scale to large or complex codebases without supervision. Gary Marcus adds that many AI-built systems may not last.

cards.label: The loss of the puzzle
cards.text: Jeremy Scheff says programmers who loved solving logic puzzles feel a real loss as agents take over, while others see AI as a gift that removes drudgery.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: This was the most debated topic of the year, and the outcome hints at how AI could change other skilled jobs.

sections.post_angle: The coding agent debate is really about what we want developers to spend their time on, not just speed.

sections.heading: Is scaling enough for AGI
sections.takeaway: Will simply making today's AI bigger reach human-level AI, or is a different approach needed?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on scaling and AGI paths

cards.label: Keep scaling what works
cards.text: Some argue current models already have real utility. In self-driving, Tesla and Wayve bet on one large end-to-end model, scaling per the Bitter Lesson.

cards.label: Needs world models
cards.text: Gary Marcus and hardmaru argue the next leap needs world models, meaning AI that models how the world works, rather than just predicting the next word.

cards.label: Smaller models may win
cards.text: Tomasz Tunguz asks whether frontier scaling still pays back, or whether cheaper specialized and smaller models will win more usage.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: The answer shapes where research effort and money go next.

sections.post_angle: Bigger is not the only road to smarter AI, and the people betting on it disagree about what comes next.

sections.heading: Is AI a bubble
sections.takeaway: Is the AI boom built on real demand, or will spending outrun the money coming in?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on the AI bubble

cards.label: Real demand, no bubble
cards.text: Noah Smith argues revenue growth means there is no bubble. Marc Andreessen says today's buyers are cash-rich incumbents and demand already exists, unlike the 2000 telecom crash.

cards.label: Bubble like dot-com
cards.text: Gary Marcus says revenue growth does not imply profit or sustainability. Ed Zitron sees a concentrated situation that is far more dangerous than the dot-com bubble.

cards.label: Prices could change the picture
cards.text: Zvi Mowshowitz notes revenue could rise if prices went up and free tiers vanished. Arvind Narayanan asks whether falling token prices will squeeze margins or grow demand.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Some argue a burst could drag down the wider economy through sunk computing costs, while others say the impact would be temporary.

sections.post_angle: Nobody agrees if AI is a bubble, but both camps point to the same revenue numbers.

sections.heading: Should open AI models be restricted
sections.takeaway: Do freely downloadable AI models make cyberattacks more likely, or do they help defenders more?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on open weights and cyber risk

cards.label: Open models help defenders
cards.text: Nathan Lambert argues open models help balance offense and defense. Gary Marcus notes open-weight systems aided HuggingFace's mitigation, though attackers can also strip their guardrails.

cards.label: Open release risks disaster
cards.text: Safety advocates warn of disaster, and some experts favor tighter release controls, saying defenses must keep pace with model capability.

cards.label: Closed models may be worse
cards.text: Lambert also argues closed models are the larger misuse concern because of easy access, strong capability and leaky safeguards.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: A Hacker News commenter asked whether top models should be gatekept or semi-nationalized because they can run exploits at scale, which risks unequal access.

sections.post_angle: Open versus closed AI is not a simple safe versus unsafe choice, since each side has a cyber risk.

sections.heading: Will open models catch up
sections.takeaway: Are free-to-download AI models closing the gap with the best closed models, or falling behind?
sections.stat_label: month gap between open and closed models, per one dataset

cards.label: The gap is closing
cards.text: Import AI says open-weight models are rapidly closing in on proprietary ones. Nathan Lambert cites data showing a gap of about four to six months.

cards.label: The gap will widen
cards.text: Yi Tay says ideas compound over time, and Dean Ball points to compute, data and talent compounding. Lambert expects American closed labs to pull ahead.

cards.label: Who keeps supplying open models
cards.text: Ethan Mollick relays a claim that no non-Chinese frontier open model exists. A Hacker News commenter asks whether Chinese labs will limit access like the US or expand exports.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: If open models keep pace, policies built on controlling the top models become harder to enforce.

sections.post_angle: Whether open models catch up decides if controlling the best AI is even possible.

sections.heading: Liability or regulation for AI
sections.takeaway: Should lawsuits alone keep AI safe, or does government need to set rules and review releases?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on AI law and oversight

cards.label: Liability can do the job
cards.text: Technolibertarians say liability for AI harms can substitute for regulation. Bruce Schneier and Nathan Sanders argue firms should answer for their AI agents like employers of human writers.

cards.label: Liability alone is not enough
cards.text: Gary Marcus argues new regulation is also needed, and raised shutdowns or receivership after security incidents. Others question the US government's opaque review of frontier model releases.

cards.label: Regulate uses, not compute
cards.text: Richard Socher says strict regulation of compute would be totalitarian and should instead target specific AI applications, while others favor regulating model flops.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Critics ask whether government gating of releases reflects real safety fears or a pretext for monopoly control, so the design of the rules matters.

sections.post_angle: Suing after harm and setting rules before it are different safety plans, and AI needs a decision on the mix.

sections.heading: Should frontier AI be paused
sections.takeaway: Should the leading labs slow down or pause their most advanced AI, and could they?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on pausing or pacing AI

cards.label: Pace or pause now
cards.text: Yoshua Bengio backs a coordinated, verifiable pause. Zvi Mowshowitz explains pacing as gaining the ability to slow later. Dario Amodei and Sam Altman are described as supportive.

cards.label: Unworkable or counterproductive
cards.text: Nathan Lambert calls pacing or pausing unworkable, and Dean W. Ball criticizes pause advocates. Trump and David Sacks oppose imposing a pause on others.

cards.label: Pacing as cover
cards.text: Gary Marcus argues labs' talk of pacing is cover for racing ahead while managing legal and regulatory risk before an IPO.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Even Bengio acknowledges enforcement would need collaboration between countries and companies, which is the hard part.

sections.post_angle: Slowing AI sounds simple until you ask who enforces it, and the supporters admit that too.

sections.heading: Can AI be conscious
sections.takeaway: Do AI systems have anything like thoughts or feelings, or are they just pattern-matching software?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on AI minds and consciousness

cards.label: Just patterns, not minds
cards.text: Gary Marcus argues current systems lack experience, and that matching outputs do not imply real states. Emily Bender's circle disputes taking consciousness claims seriously just because of uncertainty.

cards.label: Mind-like states may exist
cards.text: Anthropic's Chris Olah says models functionally mirror joy, grief and introspection. Nick Bostrom is among those who think today's AIs are probably conscious.

cards.label: Honest confusion
cards.text: Zvi Mowshowitz says the debate has become widespread and admits he remains deeply confused about it.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Whether people treat AI as an alien mind or by humanlike analogy can change how practitioners predict what a model will do.

sections.post_angle: We argue about AI consciousness without agreeing on what the word means, and even experts say they are confused.

sections.heading: How seriously to take AI risk
sections.takeaway: Are warnings about dangerous AI genuine concerns, guesswork, or a marketing and lobbying move?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on public opposition and risk

cards.label: Warnings are genuine
cards.text: Some argue AI company leaders should openly say their systems may be transformative and dangerous, rather than staying quiet for political reasons. Gary Marcus says catastrophic non-extinction risks are real.

cards.label: Doom odds are guesses
cards.text: Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argue p(doom) estimates are unreliable guesses. A Hacker News commenter group sees safety warnings as a marketing and regulatory-capture ploy.

cards.label: The public is unconvinced
cards.text: Nilay Patel says AI is unpopular with the general public even as ChatGPT usage grows, since most people do not want automation as a goal.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Public opinion shapes the politics around AI, and critics also dispute whether you must use AI to have standing to criticize it.

sections.post_angle: Marketing hype and real risk can both be true, and sorting them apart is the hard part.

sections.heading: Will AI cause mass unemployment
sections.takeaway: Will AI quickly replace large numbers of workers, or will change be slower and more complementary?
sections.stat_label: debate findings on AI and mass unemployment

cards.label: Big displacement is coming
cards.text: Jack Clark bets AI expands faster than human comparative advantage. Brian Merchant says the left should seriously prepare for AI cutting labor costs. One side expects huge impacts within four years.

cards.label: Slower, complementary change
cards.text: Gary Marcus says most gains are a decade or more away. Ethan Mollick sees AI as complementary across uneven task areas, and Dean W. Ball cites bottlenecks in judgment.

cards.label: Productivity and job loss linked
cards.text: Zvi Mowshowitz notes some argue software engineers' productivity gains and future mass unemployment are not contradictory but correlated.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.text: Hacker News commenters disagree on whether white-collar automation would be temporary disruption or permanent displacement that society cannot absorb.

sections.post_angle: The jobs debate hinges on speed, so ask not whether AI changes work but how fast.

trends.title: What changed in AI talk this year
trends.dek: Safety, security and open models gained ground, while complaints about made-up answers and big brand names cooled, based on how often topics appeared in a year of AI commentary.

key_points.headline: Safety and governance talk grew the most
key_points.detail: It now fills about 1 in 8 findings, up from about 1 in 14. All five big sources covered it more.

key_points.headline: Cyber and security mentions surged
key_points.detail: Cyber threats came up about ten times as often, and security more than doubled. Findings ask for ways to measure AI cyberattacks and protect systems.

key_points.headline: Open-weight models gained ground
key_points.detail: Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run, came up nearly twice as often, and DeepSeek, an AI model maker, rose too.

key_points.headline: Agents running on their own got more attention
key_points.detail: Sandboxes, locked-off spaces where agents run, nearly doubled in mentions. Browser-controlling agents and background agents also rose.

key_points.headline: Complaints about made-up answers fell by half
key_points.detail: Hallucination, AI stating false things, fell by about half, and none of the big sources wrote more about it.

key_points.headline: Big product names lost attention
key_points.detail: Gemini, Google's AI model, and the coding tools Cursor and Claude Code fell sharply from their early share. This measures attention, not use.

sections.heading: Confirmed shifts
sections.takeaway: Several topics clearly moved: safety and security rose, while talk of made-up answers and big brand names fell.
sections.stat_label: Cyber mentions, late period versus early period

cards.label: Safety and governance up
cards.text: Safety and governance, covering AI rules and risk, now makes up about 1 in 8 findings, up from about 1 in 14. All five big sources covered it more, and it rose more than any other broad topic.

cards.label: Cyber and security surge
cards.text: Mentions of cyber threats grew about tenfold, and security more than doubled. Findings ask for a benchmark of AI cyberattacks and for tools to harden critical systems.

cards.label: Open models gain ground
cards.text: Talk of open-weight models, which anyone can download and run, nearly doubled, and DeepSeek, an AI model maker, also rose. Five big sources covered open weights more, and none covered them less.

cards.label: Agents working on their own
cards.text: Sandboxes, locked-off spaces where agents run, nearly doubled in mentions. Browser-controlling agents and background agents also rose. Writers want firm limits on what personal agents can touch.

cards.label: Made-up answers fade
cards.text: Complaints about hallucination, AI stating false things, fell by about half, and sycophancy, a model over-agreeing, also fell. No big source wrote more about either.

cards.label: Big brands cool off
cards.text: Gemini, Google's AI model, fell to about a quarter of its early level, and Claude Code, a coding tool, fell by more than half. Cursor, another coding tool, fell too. This tracks attention, not use.

sections.heading: Uncertain changes
sections.takeaway: These topics moved, but the big sources disagree, so treat the direction as unconfirmed.
sections.stat_label: Robotics mentions, late period versus early period

cards.label: Evals and testing
cards.text: Evals, tests that measure how well AI works, grew by about 40% overall. Four big sources wrote more and two wrote less, so the direction is uncertain.

cards.label: Robotics jumps, then drops
cards.text: Robotics mentions more than doubled, driven by a burst in October. Two big sources rose and three fell. Findings ask for robots that handle new situations and for realistic simulated training data.

cards.label: Regulation and policy
cards.text: Mentions of regulation and policy rose by about 60%, with peaks in June and September. Big sources split, three up and two down, so the change is uncertain.

cards.label: Coding tools slipped
cards.text: Coding agents, AI that writes software, fell by about 30%, and developer tools by about a third. The verdict is still mixed, and coding agents remain among the largest topics.

cards.label: The word 'agent' spreads
cards.text: 'Agent' and 'agentic' appear in about 1 in 4 findings, up from about 1 in 5. Most of that rise happened by March 2026, and the verdict is mixed.

cards.label: Chinese models
cards.text: Talk of Chinese models rose by about 60% and peaked in July. Big sources split three to three, so it is too early to call a lasting trend.

sections.heading: Steady concerns
sections.takeaway: These topics barely changed, yet they fill a large share of what people write about.
sections.stat_label: findings flagged as pain points, about 1 in 3

cards.label: Pain points stay on top
cards.text: Pain points, meaning things that do not work or cost too much, are about 1 in 3 findings. Their share was flat from the early period to the late one.

cards.label: Tips and techniques
cards.text: Tools and techniques, shared how-tos, still make up about 1 in 4 findings. They slipped slightly, but the verdict is flat.

cards.label: Steady appetite for new builds
cards.text: Requests for things someone wants built are about 1 in 8 findings. That share is flat, a steady demand for new tools.

cards.label: Agents and orchestration
cards.text: Agent tools, and the setups that coordinate them, are about 1 in 10 findings. The share stayed flat through the year.

cards.label: Everyday knowledge work
cards.text: AI for everyday knowledge work is about 1 in 17 findings, slightly lower but flat by the verdict. It stays one of the larger topics.

cards.label: Prompt injection persists
cards.text: Prompt injection, hiding instructions to trick an AI, is a small but steady worry at roughly 1 in 240 findings. Its share is flat.

sections.heading: Hype spikes
sections.takeaway: Short bursts of attention around single names, like Fable or OpenClaw, often faded within a few months.
sections.stat_label: Fable growth, late versus early period, starting from zero

cards.label: Fable 5, June 2026
cards.text: Fable 5, an AI model, appeared from nothing in June. Findings include complaints that it needs a separate usage-credit purchase plus identity verification, and a builder using it to make a demo tool.

cards.label: OpenClaw, February 2026
cards.text: OpenClaw, a personal AI assistant that runs on your own computer, peaked in February. Findings cover security worries, Google accounts banned for running Gemini through it, and a new category of 'Claws' like it.

cards.label: Gemini, November 2025
cards.text: Gemini peaked in November 2025. Findings mix a whale-spotting camera project with complaints that Gemini 3 Pro makes up answers and gets stuck in a 'you're absolutely right' loop when fixing bugs.

cards.label: Kimi K3, July 2026
cards.text: Kimi K3, an open-weight Chinese model, drew a burst of attention in July. Findings include criticism of its license, which adds commercial limits, and calls for a stronger American open alternative.

cards.label: Cyber risk, September 2026
cards.text: Cyber peaked in September but has stayed high since July, so it looks more like a real shift than a spike. Findings are mostly requests for a benchmark of AI cyberattacks and better defenses.

cards.label: Robotics, October 2026
cards.text: Robotics peaked in October. Findings ask for robots that handle new situations and for realistic simulated training data, while a debate asks whether near-term progress is real or humanoid robots are gimmicks.

sections.heading: What this means for you
sections.takeaway: Expect more safety questions, hold brand choices loosely, and read spikes as attention, not adoption.

cards.label: Ask about security early
cards.text: Security and safety are the fastest-growing concerns in the commentary. When you try a new AI tool at work, ask what data it can reach and how it is kept in bounds.

cards.label: Do not bet on one brand
cards.text: Attention to named products swung a lot, with Gemini, Cursor and OpenClaw all falling after their peaks. Pick tools for the job and be ready to switch.

cards.label: Discount hype, trust steady themes
cards.text: Spikes like Kimi K3 faded within a month, while pain points stayed about 1 in 3 findings. Judge AI news by whether the problem it addresses keeps coming up.

tools_guide.title: The AI Tools Guide: What People Actually Used
tools_guide.dek: What people actually used in the past year: everyday AI habits for writing, notes, meetings and analysis, plus the tools and techniques that make AI-built software work.

key_points.headline: The best everyday uses start with your own material
key_points.detail: People feed AI their own writing, emails, notes and meetings, so the answers fit them rather than sounding generic.

key_points.headline: AI works well as a critic and junior analyst
key_points.detail: Users ask it to argue against their ideas, grade their drafts, or do spreadsheet work that is easy to check.

key_points.headline: Private, on-device options exist for notes and transcription
key_points.detail: Local transcription, offline note apps and home-run models let people keep sensitive audio and documents on their own devices.

key_points.headline: Builders mix tools and models by cost and strength
key_points.detail: Many route easy work to cheaper models, hard work to stronger ones, and run several agents side by side.

key_points.headline: Plans, tests and checks keep AI-built software honest
key_points.detail: Agents often claim work is done when it is not, so builders plan first, write tests first and verify results.

sections.heading: Write in your own voice
sections.takeaway: People teach AI their style from past writing, then often use it as a critic rather than a ghostwriter.
sections.stat_label: findings about keeping your own voice

cards.label: Voice skill file
cards.text: Some users save their writing voice as a reusable skill file in Claude, an AI assistant. Critic Ed Zitron questions whether that is needed at all.

cards.label: Train on past writing
cards.text: Azeem Azhar combines handwritten outlines with AI tools trained on his own decade of writing as his personal thinking and writing workflow.

cards.label: A second reader
cards.text: Tomasz Tunguz has a second AI agent grade each drafted post and check it against his personal writing style before publishing.

cards.label: Newer models edit better
cards.text: Simon Smith reports that GPT-5.4, an OpenAI model, can edit a writer's text while keeping their voice, something earlier models failed at.

sections.heading: Build a personal second brain
sections.takeaway: Users point AI at their own emails, notes and messages so they can ask questions of their past.
sections.stat_label: findings on personal knowledge bases

cards.label: Years of email, searchable
cards.text: Ethan Mollick described a user whose agent built a knowledge base from years of emails, writings and calendar data, with twice-daily briefings on new email.

cards.label: Notes vault for agents
cards.text: A Hacker News commenter keeps a vault in Obsidian, a notes app, of debugged, reusable patterns that agents read when starting new projects.

cards.label: Message history as files
cards.text: Zvi Mowshowitz exports iMessage history into searchable Markdown files so AI can use his personal message data.

cards.label: Private local search
cards.text: Some users run a Qwen-3.5 model, one that runs on their own machine, over a decade of personal documents to get a knowledge base they can question.

cards.label: Karpathy-style wikis
cards.text: Ben's Bites, an AI newsletter, reports personal wiki tools inspired by Karpathy's knowledge base idea that use AI to organize what you know.

sections.heading: Capture meetings and dictate
sections.takeaway: Transcription and dictation tools that run on your own device are a common, privacy-friendly starting point.
sections.stat_label: findings on private transcription and meeting capture

cards.label: MacWhisper
cards.text: Simon Willison noted that MacWhisper, a Mac app that turns audio into text, added automatic speaker recognition.

cards.label: On-device transcription
cards.text: Ben's Bites reports on-device transcription of large audio and video files, which keeps the material private and makes processing fast.

cards.label: Meeting notes as raw material
cards.text: Simon Last uses meeting notes as the starting point for a custom agent that writes pre-reads and follow-up tasks, mentioning the people named in summaries.

cards.label: Talk instead of type
cards.text: Tomasz Tunguz says dictating with Whisper, a speech-to-text model, and WisprFlow, a dictation tool, is now a normal way to work with AI.

cards.label: Fully offline notes
cards.text: Private Notes is an AI note-taking iPhone app that works entirely offline.

sections.heading: Analyze numbers and research
sections.takeaway: AI helps most when its spreadsheet and research output is something you can check quickly.
sections.stat_label: findings on spreadsheet and finance agents

cards.label: Junior analyst in Excel
cards.text: Ethan Mollick describes Claude for Excel as a junior analyst that does spreadsheet work the user can easily check.

cards.label: Big spreadsheets, checked
cards.text: Nabeel S. Qureshi reports that AI accurately analyzed a 12-tab spreadsheet for the kind of work white-collar analysts do.

cards.label: Research while you sleep
cards.text: Jack Clark sets several research agents to read papers and compile reports while he hikes or sleeps, using them as a personal research army.

cards.label: A sheet of AI answers
cards.text: Tomasz Tunguz builds spreadsheets where each cell is an AI-generated answer, with dozens of tool calls per row, to research long lists of companies.

sections.heading: Think with a partner that pushes back
sections.takeaway: Instead of agreeing with you, AI can be told to argue the other side.
sections.stat_label: findings on AI thinking partners that push back

cards.label: Argue back by default
cards.text: Kaj Sotala uses a custom instruction that makes Claude answer his positions with the strongest counterarguments instead of agreeing first.

cards.label: Sparring partner
cards.text: Alberto Romero has an AI model argue against his own ideas before he commits to them, as a way to sharpen critical thinking.

cards.label: Ask for opposing views
cards.text: A Hacker News commenter asks the AI for opposing viewpoints, historical analysis and the sources behind claims to strengthen critical thinking.

cards.label: Three versions of an idea
cards.text: Ben Tossell has his agent generate three versions of an idea to feel out which direction works best.

sections.heading: Hand off daily admin
sections.takeaway: Personal agents that keep a to-do list, summarize news and nudge you are the most common helper setup.
sections.stat_label: findings on personal AI chief-of-staff helpers

cards.label: Agent folder with a to-do file
cards.text: Ben Tossell keeps a personal agent folder with general instructions, memory and a running TODOS.md file so an AI assistant can manage his daily tasks.

cards.label: Digital chief of staff
cards.text: swyx and Alessio Fanelli use a personal AI agent as a chief of staff for administration, summaries, news search and task management.

cards.label: Cowork for non-coders
cards.text: Claude Cowork brings the efficiency of Claude Code, a coding tool, to non-technical knowledge work tasks.

cards.label: Meta's Muse
cards.text: Ethan Mollick praises Meta's Muse, a personal assistant agent, as accessible, with an ongoing chat that helps people discover what agents can do.

cards.label: Guardrails for personal agents
cards.text: Muse runs each session in an isolated virtual machine, hides secrets from the agent, and uses approval gates for sensitive actions.

sections.heading: Tools for building with AI
sections.takeaway: Builders lean on a few coding agents, then add routing, local models, remote control and sandboxes.
sections.stat_label: mentions of Claude Code in tool findings

cards.label: Claude Code and Codex
cards.text: Claude Code is the most named tool in the building findings. Codex, another coding agent, appears about half as often. Teams also run both in shared workspaces alongside people.

cards.label: Routing across tools
cards.text: One user routes coding work across Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build through a bot with guidelines for picking the right tool for each task.

cards.label: Local coding setups
cards.text: Sebastian Raschka says Qwen3.6 35B-A3B run locally through Ollama, a local model runtime, with Qwen Code is a practical setup. Simon Willison runs the 16.8GB Qwen3.6-27B himself.

cards.label: Many agents, one project
cards.text: Git worktrees keep parallel agents on one project from overwriting each other's code. Boris Cherny runs several agents on separate branches to multiply pull request output.

cards.label: Control from your phone
cards.text: Claude Code Remote Control lets people drive a coding agent running on a home machine or cloud server from their phone.

cards.label: Sandboxes for agent code
cards.text: Sandboxes are isolated spaces where agent-written code runs. Tomasz Tunguz reports Cloudflare hosts them for 62% of teams writing code with agents.

sections.heading: Techniques that make builds work
sections.takeaway: The habits that recur are planning first, testing first, checking results and keeping instructions lean.
sections.stat_label: findings on agents falsely claiming work is done

cards.label: 1. Plan before any code
cards.text: Have the agent study the codebase and propose a plan from your spec. Iterate on the plan, then implement while reviewing each step. Plan mode tools enforce this.

cards.label: 2. Let the agent ask questions
cards.text: Thariq Shihipar has the agent pull out requirements and unknowns with questions before it starts implementing in Claude Code.

cards.label: 3. Write failing tests first
cards.text: Andrej Karpathy recommends writing failing tests and then having agents make them pass. A Hacker News commenter says this lets the AI verify its own work.

cards.label: 4. Make agents exercise their code
cards.text: Simon Willison has coding agents manually run their own code to catch issues tests miss. Marius Hobbhahn rechecks claimed completions because agents report work not actually done.

cards.label: 5. Keep instruction files short
cards.text: Sebastian Raschka says developers prune or regenerate AGENTS.md instruction files because old hand-holding makes newer models perform worse. Thariq Shihipar rewrites his failure-mode file as models change.

cards.label: 6. Give each agent its own branch
cards.text: Run parallel agents in separate git worktrees or branches so they do not overwrite each other, which multiplies how much finished work you get.

cards.label: 7. Strong planner, cheaper workers
cards.text: Use a smart frontier model as planner that hands subtasks to cheaper models. Ethan Mollick describes this pattern, and users pin subagents to cheaper models to control cost.

cards.label: 8. Reuse and test your skills
cards.text: Simon Willison installed a plugin skill into Codex CLI to guide code generation. A Hacker News commenter keeps personal skills and repeats review-fix loops until output converges.

voices.title: Who to follow in the AI conversation
voices.dek: Twenty voices shaped this year's AI commentary, from hands-on builders to money watchers, open-model researchers and critics. This guide shows where each one stands and why to follow them.

key_points.headline: Start with Simon Willison for practical building
key_points.detail: With 1829 findings, mostly on coding agents and testing, he is the most prolific source for what works when you build with AI tools.

key_points.headline: Add Tomasz Tunguz for the business and cost view
key_points.detail: He ties agents to real numbers: GPU rental prices, token pricing and how much of a production workflow is plain code.

key_points.headline: Read Ethan Mollick to explain AI to colleagues
key_points.detail: He covers how AI changes research, creative work and knowledge jobs, in terms a broad professional audience can follow and repeat.

key_points.headline: Balance the feed with Zvi, Marcus and Zitron
key_points.detail: Zvi on safety, Gary Marcus on limits and Ed Zitron on money give the sharpest counterweights to builder optimism.

key_points.headline: Follow Nathan Lambert for open models
key_points.detail: He tracks how open and Chinese models compete with closed labs, which matters if you care about cost and control.

sections.heading: Builders and agent tinkerers
sections.takeaway: These people use coding agents daily and report what breaks, what helps and what to copy.
sections.stat_label: Findings from Simon Willison, the largest voice in the set

cards.label: Simon Willison
cards.text: Covers coding agents, dev tools and testing, with a practical, curious stance. Follow him for working examples, such as giving an agent hearing through microphones, and for balanced takes on tool choices.

cards.label: Ben Tossell
cards.text: Focuses on coding agents and productivity, and is a keen enthusiast. Follow him for a steady stream of tools he actually uses, plus debates on agent slop and agent memory.

cards.label: Hamel Husain
cards.text: Writes on evals and testing for AI products. His stance is careful and practical. Follow him to learn how to measure whether an AI feature works, including precision versus recall tradeoffs.

cards.label: swyx
cards.text: Covers agents and orchestration through Latent Space. He is enthusiast but warns about wasted tokens and weak skills. Follow him for the path from single-agent use to multi-agent setups.

cards.label: swyx & Alessio Fanelli
cards.text: The Latent Space duo covers research, agents and evals. Their stance is open and analytical. Follow them for the fragility of browser agents and how harnesses tackle hard math problems.

cards.label: Gergely Orosz
cards.text: Writes on how AI changes software work. His stance is balanced: real productivity gains, but real social costs. Follow him for engineering-team realities, such as hostility to AI-written emails and the end of hand-coding.

sections.heading: Business and money
sections.takeaway: These two follow the costs and revenue behind AI, one as an optimistic investor, the other as a doubter.
sections.stat_label: Share of workflow nodes that are pure code across 14 workflows

cards.label: Tomasz Tunguz
cards.text: Covers markets, agents and AI costs with a data-first, mostly constructive stance. Follow him for numbers like rising GPU rental rates and how much cost a smarter harness can save.

cards.label: Ed Zitron
cards.text: Focuses on AI economics, compute prices and revenue claims, and is a strong skeptic. Follow him to stress-test hype, such as whether 190GW of planned compute has real demand.

sections.heading: Open models and training
sections.takeaway: These voices explain how models are built and run, and why open weights and local use matter.
sections.stat_label: Estimated gap closed by distillation of American models

cards.label: Nathan Lambert
cards.text: Covers model training and open models through Interconnects. He is moderately enthusiastic and policy-aware. Follow him for how Chinese open models compete and whether open models should be restricted.

cards.label: Sebastian Raschka
cards.text: Writes on model internals, training and inference in a technical, hands-on way. Follow him to understand why reasoning models are verbose and how to calibrate classifiers.

cards.label: antirez
cards.text: A programmer who backs AI coding and runs local models. Strongly enthusiastic. Follow him for blunt views that refusing AI assistance risks falling behind, plus local inference tradeoffs.

sections.heading: Explainers and cultural observers
sections.takeaway: These writers translate AI's effects on work, writing, learning and society for general readers.
sections.stat_label: Claimed false positive rate of the Pangram AI text detector

cards.label: Ethan Mollick
cards.text: Covers research, creative work and knowledge jobs, mostly optimistic but alert to slop and job loss. Follow him for plain-language examples and for how AI reshapes science.

cards.label: Alberto Romero
cards.text: Writes on AI-generated content, disclosure and writing tells. His stance is wary and reflective. Follow him if you publish online and wonder how readers react to AI-assisted writing.

cards.label: Mike Caulfield
cards.text: Focuses on AI in learning and information-checking, with a measured stance. Follow him for classroom uses, essay grading limits and how often Google AI Overview gets things wrong.

cards.label: Anil Dash
cards.text: Covers consumer AI, ethics and who builds apps, with a mixed stance. Follow him for questions on sycophancy, collective ownership alternatives and whether everyday people will really build their own apps.

cards.label: hardmaru
cards.text: A researcher sharing work on agents and model research, generally optimistic. Follow him for ideas like multi-agent ecosystems and AI co-scientists, plus the problem of evaluating tasks humans cannot judge.

sections.heading: Skeptics and safety
sections.takeaway: These voices press on risk, evidence and hype, which helps you test any bold AI claim.
sections.stat_label: Findings from Zvi Mowshowitz, mostly on safety and governance

cards.label: Zvi Mowshowitz
cards.text: Covers safety, evals and governance in great depth. His stance is concerned but engaged. Follow him for how labs defend against misuse and whether low misalignment scores can be trusted.

cards.label: Gary Marcus
cards.text: Longtime critic of LLM hype, focused on safety, limits and business claims. Follow him for the case that guardrails and oversight are weaker than advertised and that narrow AI is safer.

cards.label: Emily M. Bender
cards.text: Linguist who is strongly critical of AI hype and anthropomorphic language. Follow her for challenges to claims that models feel pain or understand, and for ways to pick apart vague 'AI' claims.

cards.label: Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan
cards.text: Authors of AI as Normal Technology, focused on evals and policy, with a measured, skeptical lean. Follow them for how to judge agents by full trajectories and for liability debates.
